lead: A steady magnetic field does nothing to a stationary charge. Change the flux through a loop, or slide a wire across field lines, and a voltage appears — that is Faraday's law. Read the same law backwards and a coil resists any change in its own current, which is inductance. Generators, transformers, scooter ignition coils and the choke in a tube light all run on this one idea.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.6 for the magnetic field of currents and Chapter 3.1 for curl and Stokes' theorem.

blocks.text: Magnetic flux Φ is the amount of magnetic field passing through a surface. Count only the part perpendicular to the surface.

blocks.where: Φ is the flux in weber (Wb); B the magnetic field in tesla (T); dS a small area element with its outward normal, in m². For flat area A with uniform B perpendicular to it, Φ = BA, and 1 Wb = 1 T·m².

blocks.text: Faraday's law says the induced emf is the rate at which flux falls through the loop. A big steady field induces nothing; only change matters. A coil of N turns links the same flux N times.

blocks.where: ε is the induced emf in volts; N the number of turns; Φ the flux through one turn in Wb; t the time in seconds.

blocks.text: In integral form, ∮E·dl = −dΦ/dt: walk once round a closed loop, add the tangential electric field, and you get the fall in flux through the loop. Shrink the loop to a point with Stokes' theorem and the same statement becomes local, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t. A changing magnetic field creates a circulating electric field even in empty space where there is no charge at all.

The minus sign is Lenz's law. The induced current makes its own field that opposes the change in flux: flux growing, induced field against B; flux falling, induced field along B. It opposes the change, never the flux itself. That is why a magnet dropped down a copper pipe sinks slowly, and why the induced current must be paid for in mechanical work.

Take a rod of length l moving at speed v in a uniform field B, with v, B and the rod mutually perpendicular. Every charge q in the rod feels a magnetic force qv×B, so charge piles up at the ends until the electric field it sets up balances the magnetic force: qE = qvB, giving E = vB.

blocks.where: B is the field in T; l the rod length in m; v the speed in m/s, all three mutually perpendicular; ε the motional emf in volts.

blocks.text: The direction of v×B gives the force on positive charge, so it gives the positive terminal. Reverse v or reverse B and the emf reverses. If the rod moves parallel to B, v×B = 0 and the emf is zero however fast the rod moves.

Close the rod on rails through a resistor R and a current I = Blv/R flows. The field now pushes back on that current with F = BIl = B²l²v/R, opposite to the motion. To keep the rod going you supply mechanical power Fv = B²l²v²/R, which is exactly the electrical power I²R in the resistor. The drag is the price of the current.

A solid conductor sitting in a changing flux behaves like many shorted loops. Circulating eddy currents appear, heat the metal, and by Lenz drag the motion. Induction braking in trains and the damping of a moving-coil galvanometer use this; laminating a transformer core breaks up the loops and cuts the loss.

sections.h3: Inductance, energy and the LR circuit

blocks.text: A current in a coil makes flux through that same coil. Self-inductance is flux linkage per unit current.

blocks.where: NΦ is the flux linkage in weber-turns; I the current in ampere; L the self-inductance in henry (H), with 1 H = 1 Wb/A = 1 V·s/A. For a long solenoid of n turns per metre, area A and length l: L = μ₀n²Al, with μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.

blocks.text: L is fixed by the geometry and the core material, not by the current: double the current and the flux doubles with it. Two nearby coils share flux, and ε₂ = −M dI₁/dt defines the mutual inductance M in henry, the same either way round for a linear core. Transformers live on this, but that is outside this unit.

Building a current means pushing charge against the back emf, and that work is stored in the field: U = ½LI² joule. Spread over the volume, the magnetic energy density is u = B²/(2μ₀) J/m³. The energy sits in the field, not in the wire.

A circuit with source ε, resistor R and inductor L obeys ε = iR + L di/dt. Starting from zero, i = (ε/R)(1 − e^(−Rt/L)). The time constant τ = L/R is in seconds; at t = τ the current has reached 63% of its final ε/R, and by about 5τ it is effectively there. Short the source out and the current decays as i = i₀e^(−Rt/L). That dying current is what makes a spark when you break an inductive circuit.

figure.caption: Current in an LR circuit: it climbs to the final value ε/R along 1 − e^(−t/τ) and, once the source is shorted, falls back along e^(−t/τ), with τ = L/R. Both curves are the same shape, mirrored.

spec.aria: In an LR circuit the current climbs to its final value with time constant L/R and, once the source is removed, decays along the mirrored curve.

examples.question: A metal rod of length 0.2 m slides at a steady 3 m/s along two parallel rails, in a uniform magnetic field B = 0.5 T. The rod, its velocity and the field are mutually perpendicular. The rails are joined at one end by a resistor of 1.5 Ω. Find the induced emf, the current, the force needed to keep the rod moving, and check the power balance.
steps: Retarding force F = BIl = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.02 N, opposite to v.
Electrical power in the resistor: P = I²R = (0.2)² × 1.5 = 0.04 × 1.5 = 0.06 W.
Mechanical power supplied: Fv = 0.02 × 3 = 0.06 W. The two match, so energy balances.
examples.answer: ε = 0.3 V, I = 0.2 A, a retarding force of 0.02 N, and 0.06 W in the resistor — exactly the mechanical power you put in.
examples.check:
B = 0.5
l = 0.2
v = 3.0
R = 1.5
emf = B * l * v
I = emf / R
F = B * I * l
P_elec = I * I * R
P_mech = F * v
print(round(emf, 6))
print(round(I, 6))
print(round(F, 6))
print(round(P_elec, 6))

traps: Reversing Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux, not the flux. A falling flux gets a current that tries to hold the flux up, not one that pushes it down.
Using Φ instead of dΦ/dt. A loop sitting in a strong steady field has zero emf; students often report a large one.
Forgetting the perpendicular condition in ε = Blv. A rod moving along B, or a loop whose plane contains B, gives zero motional emf for that orientation.
Saying L grows with current. Flux rises in proportion to current, so L = NΦ/I stays fixed; it is set by geometry and the core.
Unit slips: mH written as H, flux in gauss·cm² instead of weber, and τ = L/R left in milliseconds without conversion.

quiz.q: State Faraday's law in words and in integral form, defining every symbol.
quiz.a: The emf induced round a loop equals the rate of fall of magnetic flux through it: ∮E·dl = −dΦ/dt, with E the electric field in V/m, dl a loop element in m, and Φ the flux in Wb through the loop.

quiz.q: Give the SI unit of magnetic flux and of self-inductance, with the base equivalence of the henry.
quiz.a: Flux: weber, 1 Wb = 1 T·m². Inductance: henry, 1 H = 1 Wb/A = 1 V·s/A.

quiz.q: What does the minus sign in ε = −dΦ/dt mean physically?
quiz.a: Lenz's law: the induced current's own field opposes the change in flux that produced it. Growing flux is fought, falling flux is supported. It never opposes the flux itself, only its change.

quiz.q: A rod moves at 5 m/s directly along a uniform magnetic field. What is its motional emf and why?
quiz.a: Zero. The force on a charge is qv×B, and v parallel to B makes the cross product zero, so no charge separation builds up.

quiz.q: A solenoid has 2000 turns per metre, cross-section 4×10⁻⁴ m² and length 0.5 m. Find its self-inductance. Take μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m.
A 12 V battery, a 6 Ω resistor and a 3 H inductor are in series. Find the time constant, the final current, and the current at t = τ.
Two identical loops of the same area, one of copper and one of a higher-resistivity alloy, are pulled out of the same field at the same speed. Compare the emf, current, force and heat produced.
quiz.a: The emf is the same for both, since it is set by Blv and the geometry. The alloy loop has larger R, so its current is smaller. Force F = BIl and heat I²R both scale with current, so both are smaller for the alloy loop: it is easier to pull out and heats less.

beyond: Not for the exam. Induction cooking uses eddy currents in the base of the vessel, and resonant wireless charging (the Qi pads on phones) is mutual inductance at a few hundred kilohertz. Eddy-current testing checks railway rails and aircraft skins for cracks without touching them; induction motors in every pump and fan are Faraday's law on a spinning rotor. Search next for resonant wireless power transfer, eddy-current non-destructive testing, and inductance extraction in PCB design.
